839.name: Invasion games: tactics and strategies when leading a team in Korfball
839.description: This unit challenges pupils to apply some tactics and strategies gained from netball and basketball to a new sport whilst focusing on respect for others and leadership skill development. Pupils will apply more advanced tactics and strategies whilst securing their understanding of a new game.
839.why: Pupils will already have developed a wide variety of skills, tactics and strategies from various games with the ball in hand. This unit requires pupils to lead and coach each other in a different game. Pupils can take these skills, experiences and positive attitudes towards participation in a range of invasion games into life with confidence and consequently lead healthy, active lives beyond school. They will also be able to spectate and socialise in and around competitive sport with an appreciation and understanding of how to play.

840.name: Health and wellbeing: yoga, pilates and mindfulness for life
840.description: This unit will develop pupils’ awareness of the restorative powers of pilates, mindfulness and other daily routines that can support holistic wellbeing and help with stress management. Pupils will experience a variety of classes and also learn about the power of breathwork.
840.why: Pupils will already have experienced a wide range of moderate to vigorous activity based fitness. This unit takes an alternative approach by considering ways to calm the mind and body but also to improve flexibility and holistic health. They will have already learnt about principles of training and this unit requires maturity and an open mind to make the most of it. Later in health and wellbeing pupils will explore exercises associated with martial arts and self-defence as they continue to discover, fine tune and commit to lifelong fitness habits.
prior: Pupils know that physical activity can improve mental wellbeing as well as physical wellbeing.
Pupils understand that holding poses requires good body tension.
Pupils are able to lead/create their own basic routines in gymnastics/dance.

841.name: Health and wellbeing: martial arts and self-defence
841.description: This unit will develop pupils’ movement competence through a variety of kata along with their emotional and spiritual development as they experience self-improvement challenges associated with martial arts and self-defence practice. Pupils will also develop their metacognition and courage.
841.why: Pupils will already have experienced a broad range of classes and fitness regimes that are widely available and popular in the local community and/ or at home. They will have learnt about physiological, psychological and socio-cultural factors connected with participation. Pupils can take these skills, experiences and positive attitudes towards participation into life with confidence and consequently lead healthy, active lives beyond school.
prior: Pupils know the importance of respect, self-control, discipline, teamwork, and communication when working in a practical environment.
Pupils understand the importance of performing movements with fluency, body awareness and control.
Pupils are able to support one another and analyse each other’s performance to improve skills and techniques.
Pupils show a willingness to try new and complex skills, whilst being supported and evaluated by others.

843.name: Dance: movie moves
843.description: This unit utilises a stylistic approach that introduces both a wider movement vocabulary and demonstrates the value of dance as an important social construct; crossing time, cultures and emphasising relevance as a lifelong activity for positive physical, emotional and social health.
843.why: This unit builds upon pupil knowledge and understanding of dances from other times and places to demonstrate its diversity and continuous evolution. By introducing a selection of established social dances, pupils are provided with the opportunity to compare and contrast, identify personal preference and consider how they might continue to engage in such activities into adulthood on a structured or ad hoc basis. It will also provide some insight into current dance cultures, deepening their cultural understanding and appreciation.
prior: Pupils can use a visual stimuli to generate original movement ideas whilst maintaining key stylistic features.
Pupils can respond consciously to the rhythm, tempo, emphasis and structure of music.
Pupils can apply focus, extension and projection using the appropriate aesthetics of the style.
Pupils can perform with accuracy and consistency.
Pupils can identify the action, spatial, dynamic or relational features within each dance style and how they complement each other.
Pupils can comment on other design features (e.g. set, costume, lighting) and how these enhance the choreography and performance.

844.name: Net and wall games: teaching others tactics and strategies in table tennis
844.description: This unit will develop core skills required for table tennis and transfer ideas, tactics and strategies from other racket sports. Pupils will focus on fair play and learn about a variety of ways to organise tournaments to help balance competition.
844.why: Pupils will already have sharpened their team working skills and ability to manage conflict in different situations. Learning how to organise tournaments and support each other to perform at their best will help cement prior learning in a new context. Pupils can take these skills, experiences and positive attitudes towards participation in a range of net and wall games into life with confidence and consequently lead healthy, active lives beyond school. They will also be able to spectate and socialise in and around competitive sport with an appreciation and understanding of how to play.
prior: Pupils know the difference between a forehand and a backhand.
Pupils understand that the ball has to bounce before it can be hit.
Pupils are able to use a drive the ball over the net to bounce on their opponent's side of the table.
Pupils show an ability to focus and accurately replicate a serve allowing the ball to hit the bat and bounce on both sides of the table.

845.name: Target games: experience lifestyle games like golf and kubb
845.description: This unit will develop pupils’ awareness of and ability to seek joy in lifestyle target games they can access in the community. Pupils will be supported to manage their emotions and apply mental preparation to closed skills to maximise performance.
845.why: Pupils will already have developed an appreciation of some of the target and garden games that promote social connection and potential catharsis from everyday life. They will have learnt simple ways to manage their emotions but this unit enables a deeper look into psychological approaches that help find a state of flow. Pupils can take these skills, experiences and positive attitudes towards participation into life with confidence and consequently seek fun ways to lead healthy, active lives beyond school.
prior: Pupils know that target games require fine motor skills and accuracy.
Pupils understand the importance of decision making and problem solving to balance higher risk shots with more consistent but potentially less impactful shots.

1654.name: Sport psychology: skill and ability
1654.description: This unit develops understanding of what skillful movement looks like and how it can be classified on different continua. It builds on the basic understanding that psychological factors can affect sporting performance in the same way physiological factors influence it.
1654.why: Pupils will already know that psychological factors connected with our brain can have an equally significant impact on performance as physiological factors relating to body systems that have been explored in previous units. This unit builds on that basic appreciation from key stage 3 PE and will ignite an interest in this growing area of sports science study. Later in sport psychology pupils will explore how to make best use of goal setting, guidance, feedback and mental preparation.
prior: Pupils have a basic understanding of what a sporting skill is and some of the features of skilful performance
Pupils show an appreciation the sports psychology is about understanding how our brain works to contribute to sporting performance

1657.name: Sport psychology: goal setting, guidance and feedback
1657.description: This unit develops understanding of how goal setting and SMART targets can be used effectively to improve performance as well as unpicking the different types of guidance and feedback that help us learn sporting skills.
1657.why: Pupils will already know what skillful performance looks like and ways to improve physiological performance by applying principles and methods of training but this unit extends basic awareness of psychological factors that can also have a huge impact on motivation to train, progress, and end results. Later in sport psychology pupils will learn how mental preparation can aid performance further.
prior: Pupils have a basic understanding of why goal setting is important for motivation and monitoring progress
Pupils show some awareness of SMART targets from PSHE/ tutor time and KS3

1660.name: Sports psychology: mental preparation for performance
1660.description: This unit develops understanding of how to best prepare our mind for competition and explores strategies like mental rehearsal, visualisation and imagery to support peak performance.
1660.why: Pupils will already know that part of warming up for competition is about getting in the right psychological state for optimum performance. This unit builds on that basic understanding from key stage 3, exposure to sports participation and following elite sport in the media. Later pupils will move on to learn about the various socio-cultural influences on participation and performance.
prior: Pupils know that we need to be in the right psychological state for optimum performance - not too relaxed and not too wired
Pupils are aware of the idea of being ‘in the zone’ and ‘choking’ under pressure in competition

1701.name: Socio-cultural influences: engagement patterns
1701.description: This unit will examine the socio-cultural factors that impact on physical activity, sport and society. Understanding engagement patterns of different social groups and factors affecting participation require an ability to interpret and analyse data.
1701.why: Pupils will already know that some sports and physical activities have lower representation from certain socio-economic backgrounds and that it is important we break down these barriers to participation. This unit cements that knowledge from key stage 3, engagement in sport in the local community and awareness of press coverage relating to different social groups. Later in socio-cultural influences pupils will study commercialisation, ethics and behaviour and make connections between the media, sportspeople, sponsors, spectators and society at large.
prior: Pupils know that some sports and activities have a bigger or smaller representation from certain societal groups (e.g. golf, swimming, lawn bowls)
Pupils understand the importance of challenging stereotypes and social injustice
Pupils are able to provide examples of minority or marginalised groups (girls etc)

1664.name: Socio-cultural influences: commercialisation
1664.description: This unit will examine the golden triangle relationship between the media, sponsors and sportspeople to help understand how sponsorship has benefits and risks for all parties as sports increasingly operate as big businesses in a billion dollar industry of professional sport.
1664.why: Pupils will already know that media exposure helps the growth and reach of different physical activities and sports. This unit builds on general knowledge and the big business of sponsorship in professional sport. Later in socio-cultural influences pupils will study ethics and behaviour with topics such as sportsmanship.
prior: Pupils know that some sports and social groups (men) get more media coverage than others
Pupils know that minority sports struggle to get exposure
Pupils understand the importance of role models in promoting sporting participation
Pupils are able to provide examples of sponsors of individuals, teams, venues and leagues
Pupils are able to provide examples of good sportsmanship and bad sporting behaviour

1667.name: Socio-cultural influences: ethics and behaviour
1667.description: This unit will examine socio-cultural factors concerned with sportsmanship, gamesmanship and deviance in sport to understand the choices made by some sportspeople and spectators.
1667.why: Pupils will already know how engagement patterns vary based on socio-economic group and the important role the media and sponsorship can play in promoting sport for all. This unit reinforces that knowledge from the preceding units and delves deeper into ethical behaviours. Links from this can be made into reasons for participation in the following health and well-being unit.
prior: Pupils know that sportsmanship involves playing fair
Pupils understand the pressure to win sometimes results in players and teams making unethical decisions and cheating
Pupils are able to provide examples of cheating or bending of the rules in sport

1670.name: Health and well-being: reasons for participation
1670.description: This unit will examine the benefits of participating in physical activity and sport on health, fitness and well-being to include physical, emotional/ mental and social factors. It will also explore the consequences of a sedentary lifestyle and implications of ill health.
1670.why: Pupils will already know about components of fitness and the long term benefits of training on their body systems from the physical training and anatomy and physiology units. This unit connects the physiological and psychological factors with a focus on everyday health and well-being. Later in health, fitness and well-being pupils will study how diet and nutrition also contribute to well-being.

1623.name: Health and well-being: diet and nutrition
1623.description: This unit will examine how much energy is needed to function and the additional requirements of a balanced diet, good hydration and potential tweaks to food consumption to allow for optimal sporting performance and energy balance.
1623.why: Pupils will already know about the relationship between exercise and diet on weight loss or gain. This unit deepens this understanding with a specific focus on nutrition and the importance of avoiding malnutrition. This unit builds on that basic appreciation from key stage 3 PE and will ignite an interest in this growing area of sports science study. Later in sport psychology pupils will explore how to make best use of goal setting, guidance, feedback and mental preparation.
prior: Pupils have a basic understanding of what a sporting skill is and some of the features of skilful performance
Pupils show an appreciation the sports psychology is about understanding how our brain works to contribute to sporting performance
threads: Think: decision making, problem solving and creative thinking
Think: knowledge of healthy, active living

1659.name: Sport psychology: goal setting, guidance and feedback
1659.description: This unit develops understanding of how goal setting and SMART targets can be used effectively to improve performance as well as unpicking the different types of guidance and feedback that help us learn sporting skills.
1659.why: Pupils will already know what skillful performance looks like and ways to improve physiological performance by applying principles and methods of training but this unit extends basic awareness of psychological factors that can also have a huge impact on motivation to train, progress, and end results. Later in sport psychology pupils will learn how mental preparation can aid performance further.
prior: Pupils have a basic understanding of why goal setting is important for motivation and monitoring progress
Pupils show some awareness of SMART targets from PSHE/ tutor time and KS3
Pupils know the difference between positive and negative feedback
threads: Think: decision making, problem solving and creative thinking

1662.name: Sports psychology: mental preparation for performance
1662.description: This unit develops understanding of how to best prepare our mind for competition and explores strategies like mental rehearsal, visualisation and imagery to support peak performance.
1662.why: Pupils will already know that part of warming up for competition is about getting in the right psychological state for optimum performance. This unit builds on that basic understanding from key stage 3, exposure to sports participation and following elite sport in the media. Later pupils will move on to learn about the various socio-cultural influences on participation and performance.
prior: Pupils know that we need to be in the right psychological state for optimum performance - not too relaxed and not too wired
Pupils are aware of the idea of being ‘in the zone’ and ‘choking’ under pressure in competition
threads: Think: decision making, problem solving and creative thinking
Think: knowledge of healthy, active living

1703.name: Socio-cultural influences: engagement patterns
1703.description: This unit will examine the socio-cultural factors that impact on physical activity, sport and society. Understanding engagement patterns of different social groups and factors affecting participation require an ability to interpret and analyse data.
1703.why: Pupils will already know that some sports and physical activities have lower representation from certain socio-economic backgrounds and that it is important we break down these barriers to participation. This unit cements that knowledge from key stage 3, engagement in sport in the local community and awareness of press coverage relating to different social groups. Later in socio-cultural influences pupils will study commercialisation, ethics and behaviour and make connections between the media, sportspeople, sponsors, spectators and society at large.
prior: Pupils know that some sports and activities have a bigger or smaller representation from certain societal groups (e.g. golf, swimming, lawn bowls)
Pupils understand the importance of challenging stereotypes and social injustice
Pupils are able to provide examples of minority or marginalised groups (girls etc)

1666.name: Socio-cultural influences: commercialisation
1666.description: This unit will examine the golden triangle relationship between the media, sponsors and sportspeople to help understand how sponsorship has benefits and risks for all parties as sports increasingly operate as big businesses in a billion dollar industry of professional sport.
1666.why: Pupils will already know that media exposure helps the growth and reach of different physical activities and sports. This unit builds on general knowledge and the big business of sponsorship in professional sport. Later in socio-cultural influences pupils will study ethics and behaviour with topics such as sportsmanship.
prior: Pupils know that some sports and social groups (men) get more media coverage than others
Pupils know that minority sports struggle to get exposure
Pupils understand the importance of role models in promoting sporting participation
Pupils are able to provide examples of sponsors of individuals, teams, venues and leagues
Pupils are able to provide examples of good sportsmanship and bad sporting behaviour

1669.name: Socio-cultural influences: ethics and behaviour
1669.description: This unit will examine socio-cultural factors concerned with sportsmanship, gamesmanship and deviance in sport to understand the choices made by some sportspeople and spectators.
1669.why: Pupils will already know how engagement patterns vary based on socio-economic group and the important role the media and sponsorship can play in promoting sport for all. This unit reinforces that knowledge from the preceding units and delves deeper into ethical behaviours. Links from this can be made into reasons for participation in the following health and well-being unit.
prior: Pupils know that sportsmanship involves playing fair
Pupils understand the pressure to win sometimes results in players and teams making unethical decisions and cheating
Pupils are able to provide examples of cheating or bending of the rules in sport

1672.name: Health and well-being: reasons for participation
1672.description: This unit will examine the benefits of participating in physical activity and sport on health, fitness and well-being to include physical, emotional/ mental and social factors. It will also explore the consequences of a sedentary lifestyle and implications of ill health.
1672.why: Pupils will already know about components of fitness and the long term benefits of training on their body systems from the physical training and anatomy and physiology units. This unit connects the physiological and psychological factors with a focus on everyday health and well-being. Later in health, fitness and well-being pupils will study how diet and nutrition also contribute to well-being.
prior: Pupils understand that regular exercise is required to build fitness
Pupils understand the different components of fitness and how they contribute to well-being and/ or sporting performance
Pupils have some appreciation of the mental and social benefits of playing sport, taking part in exercise classes or getting out in blue and green spaces
threads: Think: knowledge of healthy, active living

1625.name: Health and well-being: diet and nutrition
1625.description: This unit will examine how much energy is needed to function and the additional requirements of a balanced diet, good hydration and potential tweaks to food consumption to allow for optimal sporting performance and energy balance.
1625.why: Pupils will already know about the relationship between exercise and diet on weight loss or gain. This unit deepens this understanding with a specific focus on nutrition and the importance of avoiding malnutrition. This final unit draws together a lot of what pupils have learnt about body systems, physical training, sporting performance and more general health and well-being to promote active lifestyle choices or post-16 study to learn more.

1712.name: Exam technique and answering the extended answer questions
1712.description: This unit will explore how best to achieve top marks in the examination with a particular focus on the extended answer questions.

4128.belief: Letting the more vocal students take the lead improves team outcomes.

10155.belief: A team will still be successful as long as some of its members contribute and work hard.

7513.statement: Pupils may struggle to trust others to have their back.
7513.correction: Trust is a two-way process and something that needs to be earned and then not taken advantage of.

9043.belief: Rushing before figuring out a strategy and consequently making mistakes.
9043.statement: Rushing before figuring out a strategy and consequently making mistakes
9043.correction: Take time to plan your strategy first to avoid losing more time by being sent back to the start

10283.belief: The heart rate and breathing rate are zero when at rest.
10283.statement: Thinking the heart rate and breathing rate are zero when at rest.
10283.correction: Our body needs the energy from the oxygen we breathe in order to maintain basic living functions, hence why our heart rate is always raised above 0.

1963.belief: Confusion transferring the route from the map to real life.
1963.statement: Confusion transferring the route from the map to real life.
1963.correction: By orientating the map and holding it facing the same way relative to key features/north, you can quickly navigate around and avoid confusion every time you change direction.

4308.belief: Losing track of time or becoming distracted by the freedom of navigating without the direct supervision of a teacher.
4308.statement: Losing track of time or becoming distracted by the freedom of navigating without the direct supervision of a teacher.
4308.correction: Focus in on school values and responsibility to retain the privilege of independence.

2935.belief: A fast heart rate and feeling of nausea is dangerous and you should stop exercising.
2935.statement: A fast heart rate and feeling of nausea is dangerous and you should stop exercising.
2935.correction: This is quite normal and a sign that we are challenging our fitness. It is important to get used to the way our body feels when we start to exercise. Seek guidance if this concerns you.

611.belief: Hard work involves rushing to complete the maximum number of repetitions but with poor form.
611.statement: Believing that hard work involves rushing to complete the maximum number of repetitions but with poor form.
611.correction: Doing less movements with the correct technique will have a more positive impact on fitness than blasting out lots with poor form/range of movement.

4127.belief: Letting the most vocal pupils make all the decisions as they have the answers.
4127.statement: Letting the most vocal pupils make all the decisions as they have the answers.
4127.correction: The loudest people don't always have the best ideas. If you are a dominant character it is especially important to invest time in learning how and when to be quiet, to listen or to invite others to contribute.

11017.belief: To win you must be the quickest and race to complete tasks.
11017.statement: To win you must be the quickest and race to complete tasks
11017.correction: If we rush communication, we will not properly understand which will lead to mistakes. Even if we finish first, it will be irrelevant if the task is completed incorrectly.

3195.belief: Fundamental movement skills (FMS) are only needed at primary school.
3195.statement: fundamental movement skills (FMS) are only needed at primary school.
3195.correction: FMS underpin good movement in any activity and in wider life, so it is essential that we continue to practise and hone these basic movements.

3987.belief: Lack of cushioning with hand or foot to keep close touch control and eyes always down to look at the ball.
3987.statement: Lack of cushioning with hand or foot to keep close touch control and eyes always down to look at the ball.
3987.correction: By using kinaesthetic awareness (touch) and peripheral vision you can control the ball better with a light touch and keep your eyes up to look for space, teammates and defenders.

2128.correction: By taking the ball out into the wide channels on a pitch/court, you draw defenders out of their area and create space elsewhere to pass to your own players and make an attack on goal.

1926.belief: Confident players shooting from out of range and failing to pass when would have been a better option.
1926.statement: Confident players shooting from out of range and failing to pass when would have been a better option.
1926.correction: Getting in a strong position with a high probability of scoring if you shoot is essential. It is important to pass to a teammate in a better position rather than shoot when out of range.

4387.belief: Making loop passes are effective in attacking situations.
4387.statement: Making loop passes are effective in attacking situations.
4387.correction: Such passes are easy to intercept as they are easy to track and often don't go very far.

9024.belief: Route one - not utilising width or depth and just crowding the ball down the middle of the pitch/court.
9024.statement: Route one - not utilising width or depth and just crowding the ball down the middle of the pitch/court.
9024.correction: When attacking, it is important to use the full width of the pitch/court to draw defenders out and create space for a scoring opportunity. It is also sometimes necessary to move the ball back, before moving forward again, if the space is too crowded.

2906.belief: Failing to remain goal side whilst keeping a view on the player and the ball.
2906.statement: Failing to remain goal side whilst keeping a view on the player and the ball.
2906.correction: Failing to remain goal side of your opposition exposes yourself to an easy scoring opportunity.

6397.statement: Pupils often dribble with their head down, focusing too much on the ball and not on teammates, spaces to move into or defenders within the space.
6397.correction: Encourage pupils to develop the habit of looking up regularly to scan the area.

6929.statement: Pupils make a pass and stand still, waiting for the next ball. This is a common issue, especially in futsal, where quick transitions and movement are key.
6929.correction: After passing, always move to create an option. A great habit is to perform a give-and-go, where you pass the ball and immediately make a run to receive it back. This keeps the game fluid.

3997.belief: There is a lack of movement off the ball or teammates position themselves too close to the ball carrier therefore making it easier for the defenders to gain possession.
3997.statement: There is a lack of movement off the ball or teammates position themselves too close to the ball carrier therefore making it easier for the defenders to gain possession.
3997.correction: Pupils should always be moving off the ball to drag defenders out of positions. Pupils should also spread out and position themselves at different angles and distances from the ball carrier.

6671.statement: Pupils may often focus on power rather than accuracy when shooting. They may also make poor decisions with regards to shooting when under pressure such as facing a goalkeeper or a defender.
6671.correction: Focus on accuracy over power, working on aiming for specific targets. Pupils should practise shooting under pressure to help them make good decisions.

6875.statement: Pupils may lack the confidence to officiate a game and may struggle to take control of the game. They may be biased towards certain teams depending on who they are friends with.
6875.correction: Create a safe, encouraging environment where pupils know it is acceptable to make mistakes when refereeing Reward referees when they handle challenges made towards their decision making. Ensure pupils are respecting one another's decisions.

7048.statement: Pupils always opt to perform the most simple movements. Pupils may not like performing in front of others.
7048.correction: Give pupils time to develop their movement ideas and be creative. Share creative ideas to improve the quality of movements. Encourage pupils to present in pairs to build up their confidence in performing to one another.

3136.belief: With forward rolls, pupils may not tuck their chin, leading to discomfort. They may struggle to generate enough momentum to complete the roll.
3136.statement: With forward rolls, pupils may not tuck their chin, leading to discomfort. They may struggle to generate enough momentum to complete the roll.
3136.correction: Emphasise tucking the chin to protect the neck and practise rocking back and forth from a crouched position to develop momentum. Break each roll down into manageable steps.

8098.belief: A partner balance is a counter balance. Pupils may struggle with counter balance due to unequal weight distribution. Pupils may struggle to trust their partner.
8098.statement: Pupils may think that a partner balance is a counter balance. Pupils may struggle with counter balance due to unequal weight distribution. Pupils may struggle to trust their partner.
8098.correction: Show the difference between a partner balance and a counter balance. Pupils practice positions individually and work together to adjust the balance equally. Incorporate activities that require working together and communication to build trust.

7489.statement: Pupils struggle with spatial awareness when rotating their body. Poor posture and body alignment means pupils lose control and balance when rotating.
7489.correction: Encourage pupils to practise 90 degree rotations initially and then build up to larger rotations. Encourage pupils to use visual cues so they look at a particular spot when rotating. Encourage pupils to engage their core to maintain good posture.

5944.belief: When pupils add more content to their sequence, they can lose flow with the sequence looking unpolished. Pupils show limited variety in their locomotive elements.
5944.statement: When pupils add more content to their sequence, they can lose flow with the sequence looking unpolished. Pupils show limited variety in their locomotive elements.
5944.correction: Practise the sequence slowly at first, focusing on smooth transitions between movements and balances. Encourage pupils to be creative and add variety to their locomotive movements throughout the sequence.

6414.belief: When pupils evaluate each others performances, they overlook the important details such as performing with control, extension, flow and accurate timing.
6414.statement: When pupils evaluate each others performances, they overlook the important details such as performing with control, extension, flow and accurate timing.
6414.correction: Make sure pupils are using the worksheet to help them evaluate the sequences so that they focus on the fundamentals that make a sequence high quality.

3935.belief: When jumping from apparatus, pupils may rush the jump and not be balanced before they take off. Pupils may land with stiff knees or poor body position.
3935.statement: When jumping from apparatus, pupils may rush the jump and not be balanced before they take off. Pupils may land with stiff knees or poor body position.
3935.correction: Always check balance and engage the core before jumping. Ensure a solid stance before jumping. Pupils should bend their knees to absorb impact on landing and make sure their weight is centered over their feet.

7338.statement: Pupils struggle to coordinate their take off on to the springboard. Pupils land on the springboard with their heels.
7338.correction: Use a short run up to develop good take off technique focusing on 1 foot to 2 feet on the springboard. Pupils should always land on the balls of their feet to get more lift from the springboard.

6448.statement: Pupils fear running at speed to jump on to the springboard or are reluctant to jump on to a vault/box top. Pupils have poor technique on the springboard. Pupils fear straddling the box.
6448.correction: Build confidence by breaking the skill down. Practise without the box top or with a lower box gradually increasing height. Develop good foot positioning on the springboard before adding in the box top. Pupils could straddle on to the box first.

6889.statement: Pupils often link pieces of apparatus together e.g. benches attached to a table which limits the use of space and options for pathways. Pupils rush to create balances that are not of high quality.
6889.correction: Encourage pupils to place apparatus in spaces to allow them to explore interesting pathways and to be able to use each piece of apparatus in creative ways. Peer assessment of balances can encourage refinement and increase quality of pupils work.

11115.belief: When working in bigger groups, there may be issues with group dynamics as pupils have to negotiate which movements they will use. Not all pupils in the group may be able to perform the movements.
11115.statement: When working in bigger groups, there may be issues with group dynamics as pupils have to negotiate which movements they will use. Not all pupils in the group may be able to perform the movements.
11115.correction: Pupils could delegate a leader or be encouraged to listen to each other when working in bigger groups. Pupils may have to consider adapting their routines to help other members of their group.

7205.statement: Pupils rush their feedback and don't give detailed advice to enable pupils to make improvements. Pupils may rush to refine their routines without carefully considering how they can make improvements.
7205.correction: Provide numerous examples of high quality feedback throughout to highlight your expectations. Ensure that pupils take care over the details to improve their routine.

8031.belief: They need a big swing and to serve overarm.
8031.statement: Pupils think they need a big swing and to serve overarm.
8031.correction: When we watch pro tennis or other racket sports it looks like you need a huge swing and lots of power but when you are starting out you will get more success with a slow and controlled swing. Pickleball (like badminton) starts with an underarm serve.

7273.statement: Pupils often stand behind the ball and hit up at it rather than moving their body to get into a better position.
7273.correction: You need to move your feet quickly to get to the side of the ball to use a smooth U shaped swing on the forehand or backhand and hit through the ball towards the net.

7935.belief: It's ok to stop and stand mid-court.
7935.statement: Pupils think that it's ok to stop and stand mid-court.
7935.correction: It is essential to return to the middle of the court and split step as your opponent hits the ball to load elastic energy in your legs to be able to move quickly. Don't get caught standing between the baseline and non-volley line on approach to net.

8044.belief: They need to swing hard at volleys.
8044.statement: Pupils think they need to swing hard at volleys.
8044.correction: When approaching the net to volley you already have momentum moving forwards into the ball which adds power so a more effective technique is to block and sometimes even cushion the pace out of the ball whilst angling it back over the net.

7663.belief: The best way to win is to hit ithe ball harder.
7663.statement: Pupils think the best way to win is to hit ithe ball harder.
7663.correction: Sometimes just keeping the ball in and waiting for your opposition to make a mistake is the best way to win points, but it is also helpful to disrupt the rhythm by varying pace/spin, breaking the angle or using disguise to wrong foot your opposition.

8378.belief: Winning is the most important thing.
8378.statement: Pupils think that winning is the most important thing.
8378.correction: Learning to value a fair competition and choosing to lose in preference to cheating to win or only playing opponents you know you can beat, is a much more rewarding outlook.

7696.belief: The chest pass is only used for shorter distances.
7696.statement: Pupils think the chest pass is only used for shorter distances.
7696.correction: The chest pass is a very versatile technique that can be used for short and longer distances. It works well as a technique to pass when aiming for the space a teammate is moving into.

491.belief: An attacker should move as as soon as their teammate catches the ball.
491.statement: An attacker should move as as soon as their teammate catches the ball.
491.correction: A feint is an effective way to create space as we wait for the ball handler to present the ball ready to make the pass, rather than moving too early and the defender being able to catch up with you.

3417.belief: A GS is a static position.
3417.statement: A GS is a static position.
3417.correction: The GS can move out of the goal circle to create space for the GA to drive in and receive the ball. A shooter position requires dynamic movements such as power to jump for a rebound.

2215.belief: Defending in netball is mainly a role when your opponent has the ball.
2215.statement: Defending in netball is mainly a role when your opponent has the ball.
2215.correction: Defending occurs in all positions and each player needs to track their opponent to try to deny them the opportunity to receive a pass.

8086.belief: The opposite team to the scoring team take the following center pass.
8086.statement: Pupils think that the opposite team to the scoring team take the following center pass.
8086.correction: The center pass is alternated throughout the game regardless of which team scores.

7872.belief: When they go offside or do footwork they have to stand out of play as this is a penalty pass.
7872.statement: Pupils think when they go offside or do footwork they have to stand out of play as this is a penalty pass.
7872.correction: Both of these infringements do not include another player so a free pass is awarded. If a player obstructs or contacts an oppositing player a penalty pass is then awarded.

6334.correction: Whilst some pupils can count music accurately, it can be an additional level of challenge for others and divert them from the task in hand. Most pupils will naturally 'feel' the music and be able to respond to the tempo and rhythm appropriately.

8479.statement: Pupils are all uncomfortable with physical contact.
8479.correction: Contact must involve respect. Care should be taken to ensure any touch is appropriate. Most pupils are sensitive to this and respond appropriately. Teachers can guide this by identifying how contact should be made, e.g. touch toe to toe.

345.belief: When applying dynamics, fast actions are always strong.
345.statement: When applying dynamics, fast actions are always strong.
345.correction: We often tend to combine fast actions with strength and slow actions with softness but this isn't always the case. Slow and strong could suggest great effort against resistence, and fast and light actions communicate fluidity and ease.

5463.belief: When performing a 'pulling' counterbalance, pupils should hold hands.
5463.statement: When performing a 'pulling' counterbalance, pupils should hold hands.
5463.correction: There are many ways to perform 'pulling' counterbalances other than using hands, but if doing so, pupils should clasp one another's wrists to make a more secure connection.

67.belief: Not accepting the first action that a pupil offers is likely to put them off.
67.statement: Not accepting the first action that a pupil offers is likely to put them off.
67.correction: Challenging pupils to generate more than one response, or to find ways to refine their actions, before making their final selection, enables pupils to develop their creativity and understanding of choreographic and performance skills.

6883.statement: Pupils are likely to focus on people who are famous.
6883.correction: It is entirely possible that pupils are naturally drawn to people who are famous, but it is still feasible to identify the qualities and behaviours that have made them successful such as hard work, determination or courage.

8420.statement: Pupils often throw with a stiff arm and do not step into their pass with the opposite foot, resulting in inaccurate and unbalanced throws.
8420.correction: Ensure that pupils can throw with the correct technique from a static position before adding any movement.

8437.statement: Pupils may try to hit the ball too hard when playing competitively. Pupils may be dishonest when scoring their own games in the competitions.
8437.correction: Emphasise the importance of playing accurate and controlled shots rather than focusing on hitting the ball hard. Remind pupils of the importance of respect and playing by the rules in competitive situations, and to just focus on trying their best.

7503.statement: Pupils struggle with their release point when bowling underarm which results in an illegal bowling action. Pupils are too slow to throw from backstop to first base when trying to run the batter out.
7503.correction: Pupils should focus on a smooth pendulum action when bowling to ensure that the ball is bowled between knee and head height and to the side of the batter. When backstop has the ball, focus on a flat, hard throw to first base to run the batter out.

6874.statement: Pupils lack the confidence to make decisions, often worrying what their peers might say if they don't agree with a decision.
6874.correction: Provide pupils with reassurance that it is acceptable to make mistakes and ensure everyone in the group is respectful of decisions made by officials.

6931.statement: Pupils often make slow decisions when covering each other due to lack of confidence. They also panic when they are under pressure in a game situation.
6931.correction: Encourage quick and clear communication using captains and coaches to help players make good decisions.

6119.belief: All the power in sprinting comes from the legs and not use their arms enough when performing.
6119.statement: Pupils may believe that all the power in sprinting comes from the legs and not use their arms enough when performing.
6119.correction: Power in sprinting is created by a combination of powerful legs and arms working simultaneously, hence why sprinters often have muscular arms as well as legs.

7284.statement: Pupils start long distance running too fast through a mixture of excitement, copying each other and overestimating the pace they can maintain.
7284.correction: Emphasise the need to calculate and find a suitable pace and consider how sustainable a fast pace is going to be.

5467.belief: When perfroming the long jump, many pupils take a long step into the pit which means they land with one foot in front of the other which reduces the distance they achieve.
5467.statement: When perfroming the long jump, many pupils take a long step into the pit which means they land with one foot in front of the other which reduces the distance they achieve.
5467.correction: Pupils should be taught to land with feet parallel by bringing the take-off foot through and in front of them so that no distance is lost and they achieve a maximal score.

7096.statement: Pupils are often quick to focus their feedback on something which went wrong or needs improvement, without considering the impact of identifying what is also being performed well.
7096.correction: Pupils can use methods such as the 'feedback sandwich' which encourages them to think about identifying positive aspects of performance as well as areas for improvement.

7320.statement: Pupils often struggle with combining the different phases of the triple jump in the correct sequence.
7320.correction: Build up to the full performance gradually, without an approach to begin with and gradually introducing one at walking pace and then jogging pace. Have a partner coach the performer to check their coordination and technique to quickly correct errors.

4083.belief: When learning the scissors technique, pupils often use an incorrect take-off foot, choosing to jump from the foot closest to the bar instead of the foot furthest away.
4083.statement: When learning the scissors technique, pupils often use an incorrect take-off foot, choosing to jump from the foot closest to the bar instead of the foot furthest away.
4083.correction: Allow pupils to practise jumping off their right foot, then their left, before performing the full action to establish which they prefer to take off with. Be observant during full performances and be ready to suggest a pupil changes approach side.

6450.belief: There may be pupils who feel confident and enthusiastic and want to take over all officiating and not allow others to do so.
6450.statement: There may be pupils who feel confident and enthusiastic and want to take over all officiating and not allow others to do so.
6450.correction: All pupils should take some role in officiating. Assign roles such as scorecard keeper and person in charge of reading the aims and rules at each event.

7097.statement: Pupils may be quick to get over emotional when challenged with being the official, leading to inaccurate, unfair or even biased decisions being made.
7097.correction: Pupils must learn to regulate their emotions when acting as the official to ensure competition is fair.

8680.belief: Putting is a unique action and pupils often unwittingly revert to a throwing action which can lead to injury. Throwing is against the rules/regukations, thus it is also often illegal in competitions.
8680.statement: Putting is a unique action and pupils often unwittingly revert to a throwing action which can lead to injury. Throwing is against the rules/regukations, thus it is also often illegal in competitions
8680.correction: Encourage the key technical points of holding the shot against the neck throughout the preparation and pushing the shot phases first, alsongide the key point about a straight wrist and extending elbow following behind at all times.

1805.belief: A common mistake pupils make is using a 'bowling' style of throw in which the throwing arm remains straight throughout the action.
1805.statement: A common mistake pupils make is using a 'bowling' style of throw in which the throwing arm remains straight throughout the action.
1805.correction: Ask pupils to think about pulling the javelin through, with the elbow leading first.

3563.belief: Hurdles is daunting for many pupils who may fear hitting the hurdle, falling or getting hurt, which are justifiable concerns. This causes them to do things such as stutter their approach or even stop.
3563.statement: Hurdles is daunting for many pupils who may fear hitting the hurdle, falling or getting hurt, which are justifiable concerns. This causes them to do things such as stutter their approach or even stop.
3563.correction: Be careful to provide hurdles which are achievable for all abilities and gradually allow pupils to build confidence and progress to higher hurdles when ready, rather than expect them to hurdle the full height.

7077.statement: Pupils often perform relay changeovers with the receiver standing still until they receive the baton, then accelerating into their sprint.
7077.correction: Changeovers should be performed at high speed. The receiver begins to accelerate at just the right moment to high speed but not too far ahead of the incoming runner. This will be different for each pupil (~3.5m is a good point to work from).

5587.belief: You can only play target games with another person.
5587.statement: You can only play target games with another person.
5587.correction: Target games can be played with other people and by yourself.

8995.belief: You can roll the ball from any height.
8995.statement: You can roll the ball from any height.
8995.correction: It is more accurate to roll the ball from a lower position which is achievied by bending your knees.

636.belief: It is best to hit a ball with very little power.
636.statement: It is best to hit a ball with very little power.
636.correction: You need to use some power to hit the ball to allow the ball to bounce, especially if it is a soft ball or some rolled up socks.

2507.belief: When dribbling the ball, your head should look at it.
2507.statement: When dribbling the ball, your head should look at it.
2507.correction: When dribbling, your head should look up to develop kinaesthetic awareness and maintain ball control, without bumping into anything in the working area/environment.

3062.belief: Focus on pushing off from the ground with maximum force for height or distance and prioritising speed of execution.
3062.statement: Focus on pushing off from the ground with maximum force for height or distance and prioritising speed of execution.
3062.correction: The most critical skill for precision, confidence and long term athletic health is the ability to efficiently absorb and redirect force upon landing. A powerful jump with a weak or uncontrolled landing risks injury.

5437.belief: Perfect balance means not moving at all.
5437.statement: Perfect balance means not moving at all.
5437.correction: Balance is actually a constant series of tiny corrections. Your brain and muscles are in a non-stop conversation, making micro-adjustments to keep your centre of gravity over your base. This happens in static and dynamic balances.

10317.belief: Throwing something with more force will make it more accurate.
10317.statement: Throwing something with more force will make it more accurate.
10317.correction: Increased force usually reduces accuracy unless the technique is correct (stance, grip, arm swing and follow through).

9659.belief: Struggling with coordination means you are clumsy, careless or simply not trying.
9659.statement: Struggling with coordination means you are clumsy, careless or simply not trying.
9659.correction: During adolescence, rapid growth spurts cause a temporary mismatch as limbs are longer than the brain thinks they are, which causes a calibration error. Consequently, it is essential to keep practising fine and gross motor skills as you grow.

5447.belief: You always perform a motif at the same speed.
5447.statement: You always perform a motif at the same speed.
5447.correction: Often you adapt your motif to the speed of the music you are dancing to.

5091.belief: Once a motif is created it has to stay the same and can't be adapted.
5091.statement: Once a motif is created it has to stay the same and can't be adapted.
5091.correction: You can always adapt a motif by changing the actions, space or dynamics.

2165.belief: A dance routine cannot repeat any motifs within it.
2165.statement: A dance routine cannot repeat any motifs within it.
2165.correction: A dance routine can use repeated phrases of movement, for example, when a chorus comes back on within the song.

3525.belief: Honesty is required at all time, not just when poeple are watching.
3525.statement: Honesty is required at all time, not just when poeple are watching.
3525.correction: Honesty is always important because it shows who you really are. Being honest builds trust, helps you feel proud of your choices and means that you do the right thing, even when no one is watching.

4903.belief: You only need to use safe lifting technique if the item is heavy.
4903.statement: You only need to use safe lifting technique if the item is heavy.
4903.correction: Whenever we are bending down to something pick up, we still must bend from the knees and protect our back to prevent possible straining from leaning over.

4859.belief: You need either logical thinking or creative thinking in isolation.
4859.statement: You need either logical thinking or creative thinking in isolation.
4859.correction: When you use both logical and creative thinking together, you can plan clearly, adjust your approach and find the best solution, even when a task is challenging.

4865.belief: You need to go to a gym to build muscle strength and endurance.
4865.statement: You need to go to a gym to build muscle strength and endurance.
4865.correction: Body weight exercises, that require little or no equipment, can be performed in a safe space in your own home and can be incredibly effective at building muscular strength, endurance and general fitness.

10379.belief: Training must be at maximal effort to push past the pain.
10379.statement: Training must be at maximal effort to push past the pain.
10379.correction: The focus should be on vigorous activity. Listen to your body and work at a high intensity, but one that is dicated by your current fitness levels and the sort of exercise you are used to.

8740.belief: A racing heart and feeling of breathlessness means you need to slow down.
8740.statement: A racing heart and feeling of breathlessness means you need to slow down.
8740.correction: You need to build up gradually and pace yourself at the start of a run, but feeling out of breath and a racing heart rate is normal during sub-maximal exercise.

3423.correction: Flexibility is important for performance in any activity/sport. Essentially, it is important for every day health and wellbeing, especially to avoid lower back pain and poor posture.

11028.belief: Winning is the only metric of success and losing is always bad.
11028.statement: Winning is the only metric of success and losing is always bad.
11028.correction: You can make improvements to your own/your team's performance in many different ways, regardless of the outcome of a competition.

7242.statement: Pupils seek the easiest opportunity to guarantee a win.
7242.correction: Winning an unfair or unbalanced race/competition is a hollow victory and greater satisfaction comes from winning a balanced contest where both individuals/teams have a good chance of winning.

10142.belief: Target games must be played against people of similar ability or previous experience for it to be a fair competition.
10142.statement: Target games must be played against people of similar ability or previous experience for it to be a fair competition.
10142.correction: Conditions can be put on specific players in target games to balance the competition, regardles of their ability or previous experience.

848.belief: If you can't see the outcome of your performance, you are unable to learn how to improve.
848.statement: If you can't see the outcome of your performance, you are unable to learn how to improve.
848.correction: Receiving feedback from teammates and other pupils about your performance will enable you to learn and make progress.

10553.belief: Upper body strength is the primary fitness component required for seated volleyball.
10553.statement: Upper body strength is the primary fitness component required for seated volleyball.
10553.correction: Core strength is fundamental to play seated volleyball effectively as it enables players to maintain their body position in the preparation and executon of skills throughout the game.

10362.belief: All tournaments must focus solely on the outcome/winner of competition.
10362.statement: All tournaments must focus solely on the outcome/winner of competition.
10362.correction: In order for all participants to feel included, tournaments can take many forms and be adapted so that everyone can enjoy an appropriate level of challenge.

6013.statement: Pupils attack territory down the middle of the court or pitch and it becomes crowded.
6013.correction: By using accurate passing and movement of the ball out wide, you draw defenders out and create more space to invade. Similarly, by moving the ball back and then forward again, you can create more space.

8617.statement: Pupils wait until a defender is too close before trying to make a pass and consequently lose possession often.
8617.correction: By getting control of the ball quickly, looking up to find teammates in space and passing before a defender gets too close you can keep possession better.

8587.statement: Pupils use both sides of the stick like they see in ice-hockey.
8587.correction: In field hockey you are only allowed to use the flat side of the stick. If the ball touches the other side or your foot it is a foul.

10157.belief: Teams don't discuss tactics properly and instead focus on just wanting to play a game.
10157.statement: Teams don't discuss tactics properly and instead focus on just wanting to play a game.
10157.correction: Forming a number of predetermined plans can be an effective way to capitalise on set play situations and being aware of which team members are the biggest threat to the opposition can leave other players more open.

6198.statement: Some pupils commit to zone defence but others get distracted into chasing the ball, therefore moving out of position.
6198.correction: It is essential that all team members follow the same defensive strategy of player-to-player or zonal marking to avoid leaving big gaps.

8461.statement: Pupils are unable to adjust their team tactics based on the situation.
8461.correction: Changing the way you play as a team to include formation, tactics and roles of different players can have a huge impact on the game and a shift in momentum that disrupts your opposition.

6908.statement: Pupils make a big touch so they don't have close control of the ball. Pupils slow down after turning with the ball.
6908.correction: Encourage pupils to keep the ball close to the body so they have control at all times. Pupils should explode after the turn pushing off with their standing leg.

8045.belief: They need to take multiple touches before passing the ball.
8045.statement: Pupils often think they need to take multiple touches before passing the ball.
8045.correction: Encourage pupils to make quick decisions using one or two touch passes, and encourage pupils to scan before receiving the ball so they know where to pass to next.

6645.statement: Pupils often find passing over distance much harder and try to kick the ball too hard. Often pupils are too close together so no one is in a wide position to aim for.
6645.correction: Encourage pupils to slowly increase the distance at which they pass so they maintain control and accuracy. Pupils should be encouraged to adopt wide positions when attacking, stretching defenders to create space.

7435.statement: Pupils struggle to make quick decisions and perform skills correctly when defenders are present and adding pressure.
7435.correction: Remind players to scan before receiving the ball. Use mini games or time limits in tasks so pupils are used to performing under pressure.

10152.belief: When teaching the offside rule, pupils often struggle with understanding a player is offside when the ball is passed to them not when they receive it.
10152.statement: When teaching the offside rule, pupils often struggle with understanding a player is offside when the ball is passed to them not when they receive it.
10152.correction: Use cues to show the moment the ball was passed. For example, you could ask the pupils to freeze just as the ball is passed to determine whether they are offside or not.

6876.statement: Pupils may lack confidence when officiating and fear making incorrect decisions. They may also struggle with peer pressure and be tempted to change their decisions.
6876.correction: Encourage pupils to make clear, firm decisions and remind them that mistakes are part of learning. Teach referees to stand by their decisions and use short, clear explanations. Also ensure the players are respectful of those decisions.

7705.belief: A circuit has to involve exercises in a circle.
7705.statement: Pupils think a circuit has to involve exercises in a circle.
7705.correction: A circuit is a series of exercises done a specific order but does not have to be set up like a circle.

242.belief: Anaerobic exercise is only useful for improving your ability to run fast.
242.statement: Anaerobic exercise is only useful for improving your ability to run fast.
242.correction: Anaerobic training can also build muscular strength, power, endurance and improve body composition. All of these can benefit your performance in many different sports not just running.

7607.belief: Aerobic training is only relevant for endurance athletes like long distance runners.
7607.statement: Pupils think aerobic training is only relevant for endurance athletes like long distance runners.
7607.correction: Aerobic training is useful for any athletes that play sports that last longer than 20 minutes, e.g. rugby, netball football, hockey.

7706.belief: Circuit training is solely to improve components of fitness but not for developing skilled sports performance.
7706.statement: Pupils think that circuit training is solely to improve components of fitness but not for developing skilled sports performance.
7706.correction: While circuit training is great for improving components of fitness, it can also be designed to develop sport-specific skills. For example, in basketball, a circuit can include dribbling, shooting and passing stations, alongside fitness exercises.

7919.belief: They should just include their favourite exercises in their own circuit.
7919.statement: Pupils think they should just include their favourite exercises in their own circuit.
7919.correction: Exercises should be selected and used to target and imporove specific areas of weakness, e.g. certain muscle groups, a components of fitness or a sport specific skill you need more practice at.

7670.belief: Body adaptations will occur and stay from training only once.
7670.statement: Pupils think that body adaptations will occur and stay from training only once.
7670.correction: Body adaptations like stronger muscles or better endurance don’t happen after just one training session. To see improvements, you need to train regularly. If you stop training, your body can start to lose those gains – this is called reversibility.

6373.statement: Some pupils may dominate the discussion with less confident pupils unwilling to take their turn at leading. Pupils might take too long explaining and not leave enough time to practise.
6373.correction: Select the numbers carefully so that pupil 1 and 2 are more confident and can model teaching first, giving less confident pupils time to get used to this process. Stress the importance of practise time and keep explanations concise.

7571.belief: When pupils are teaching, they do not use the additional materials and therefore provide incorrect teaching points or unsuitable adaptations for their group.
7571.statement: When pupils are teaching, they do not use the additional materials and therefore provide incorrect teaching points or unsuitable adaptations for their group.
7571.correction: Ensure pupils are using the additional materials to support their understanding of each skill and make sure they know how to provide adaptations so that everyone in the group can achieve success when performing the skill.

6716.statement: Pupils often forget to tuck their head when performing forward and backward rolls causing a rough landing or strain on their neck.
6716.correction: The chin should be tucked gently into the chest looking at their stomach. This will protect the neck and keep the head aligned.

5466.belief: When performing in unison, some students may be slightly ahead or behind affecting overall synchronisation. If pupils don't move at the correct intervals in canon, the sequence looks uncoordinated.
5466.statement: When performing in unison, some students may be slightly ahead or behind affecting overall synchronisation. If pupils don't move at the correct intervals in canon, the sequence looks uncoordinated.
5466.correction: Use a clear count-in or rhythm (e.g. counting beats out loud or clapping) and practise slowly before increasing speed.

5460.belief: Performing group routines often means some members of the group may struggle with the choreography and therefore feel self-conscious and demotivated.
5460.statement: Performing group routines often means some members of the group may struggle with the choreography and therefore feel self-conscious and demotivated.
5460.correction: Stress to each group the importance of adapting choreography to suit the needs of everyone in the group. For example, some pupils could perform backward rolls whilst others perform a more basic roll. Or everyone may change the skill they perform.

7316.statement: Some pupils may struggle with the choreography, leading to frustration and disengagement.
7316.correction: Differentiate within the choreography so that pupils have choices over the skills they perform. If you would like all pupils to perform the same skill, make sure this skill is accessible for all pupils.

8586.statement: Pupils use short steps and run through as they hit the shuttle which leaves them out of position for the next shot.
8586.correction: Using long lunges and recovering back to the middle of the court quickly between each shot reduces the space and options available to your opposition.

7246.statement: Pupils serve towards the middle of the court which is easy to return.
7246.correction: Aiming their serve to force a defensive shot from their opponent is a much stronger way to start the point.

6782.statement: Pupils hold the racket like a frying pan and squat lower and lower to hit overhead clears.
6782.correction: A shake hand grip and sideways stance is required to get power and accuracy into shots, but you also need to know when it is necessary to hit underarm rather than trying to hit everything above the head.

6784.statement: Pupils hold their index finger up towards the shaft of the racket to try to get more control.
6784.correction: Letting your index finger point up the back of the grip feels like it is helping with control, but break this habit fast to prevent this technique from limiting your progress to the full range of shots that are possible with a shake hands grip.

6744.statement: Pupils get confused about which side to serve from and who serves next.
6744.correction: A server keeps serving after winning a point and they alternate sides each point —from the right if their score is even and left if it is odd. If the opposition wins a rally, they earn a point and the service with the other partner serving next.

6176.statement: Pupils blame each other and lose focus rather than remaining positive and regrouping.
6176.correction: Remind pupils that the balanced teams mean everyone should have an equal chance of winning. Hence it is the pair who gel the best and work hard to win as many points as possible across all their matches that will win.

646.belief: It is better to move with the ball in one hand and score a try with one hand.
646.statement: It is better to move with the ball in one hand and score a try with one hand.
646.correction: Despite it perhaps being more comfortable to have the ball in one hand (or under the arm) when running, it does not keep the ball as safe and therefore increases the risk of dropping the ball and therefore your team losing possession.

2467.belief: I don't need to practice passing because I can already catch well and have good technique.
2467.statement: I don't need to practice passing because I can already catch well and have good technique.
2467.correction: Passing isn’t just about mechanics, it’s also about teamwork. Practicing with different teammates helps improve subtle communication, like eye contact and timing, and allows you to understand how others prefer to receive the ball.

2772.belief: Evading space is solely about the ball carrier getting past the defender.
2772.statement: Evading space is solely about the ball carrier getting past the defender.
2772.correction: In reality, a supporting runner's positioning often determines whether an attacker breaks the gain line. A well-timed support line can draw defenders, create passing opportunities, or make a dummy pass more effective.

3947.belief: A kick is only good if it is kicked far.
3947.statement: A kick is only good if it is kicked far.
3947.correction: Kicking a ball successfully involves accuracy and tactical placement to find space, kicking into touch or to allow one of your team to catch and maintain possession.

5929.belief: Pupil think that if they go in to tackle at the legs they will get kicked in the face.
5929.statement: Pupil think that if they go in to tackle at the legs they will get kicked in the face.
5929.correction: If you tackle low, with your head to the side and wrap their legs with your arms, they’ll go down safely and you won’t get kicked.

5578.belief: Play needs to be stopped by the referee at every single rule break.
5578.statement: Play needs to be stopped by the referee at every single rule break.
5578.correction: Not every rule break means the game has to stop. The referee can play advantage, keeping the game flowing and more enjoyable. However, dangerous play, like high tackles, must be dealt with straight away to keep everyone safe.

858.correction: Capoeira is based on challenging your opponent, but in a game-like scenario. This is why performers are called 'players'.

859.belief: In Capoeira you use pre-recorded music.
859.statement: In Capoeira you use pre-recorded music.
859.correction: In Capoeira the music is played live and the tempo and style of the music dictates the style of the game that will be played.

9608.belief: The steps learnt have to be performed in a set order.
9608.statement: The steps learnt have to be performed in a set order.
9608.correction: In the Lindy Hop, the dancers' personal style and flair was highly prized so they would find new and inventive ways of arranging and performing the key actions seen it this style.

10058.belief: If supporting another person you should be as far away from them as possible.
10058.statement: If supporting another person you should be as far away from them as possible.
10058.correction: To support another person effectively, the performers need to be in close proximity with the 'supporter' adopting a wide base and using the large muscle groups to power the action.

3493.belief: Hip Hop is a dance style.
3493.statement: Hip Hop is a dance style
3493.correction: Hip Hop is a generic term for a number of dance styles that are heavily influenced by street culture (DJing, graffiti, rapping). There are a large number of subdivisions which vary according to time and place of origin.

3492.belief: Hip Hop culture focuses on 'disrespecting' your opponent and mocking them.
3492.statement: Hip Hop culture focuses on 'disrespecting' your opponent and mocking them.
3492.correction: As in all competitive settings, the performers are trying to succeed and employ a variety of strategies to do so, but this also includes congratulating others on their successes and supporting those who are developing their skills.

4936.belief: New games are often hindered by preexisting rules and scoring systems which remain the basis and stunt creativity.
4936.statement: New games are often hindered by preexisting rules and scoring systems which remain the basis and stunt creativity.
4936.correction: Pupils must think outside the box and forget about pre-existing activities when creating their own games. It is important to instil the confidence to try something new even if it doesn't work.

689.belief: Blaming others for mistakes and rushing rather than planning first and taking care over the approach.
689.statement: Blaming others for mistakes and rushing rather than planning first and taking care over the approach.
689.correction: Less overall time is lost if you invest in planning, negotiating and caring for each other.

5592.belief: All players are desperate to get the opposition's treasure so they have a high risk of getting caught and neglecting the protection of their own treasure.
5592.statement: All players are desperate to get the opposition's treasure so they have a high risk of getting caught and neglecting the protection of their own treasure.
5592.correction: Let pupils do it however they like first but then give time to regroup and plan a smarter team strategy.

9042.belief: Rushing to complete the task and therforemfailing to listen to, or consider, all group members.
9042.statement: Rushing to complete the task and therforemfailing to listen to, or consider, all group members.
9042.correction: Together Everyone Achieves More, it is essential to work as a TEAM and ensure everyone is valued.

3096.belief: Forgetting to align north on the compass with north on the map before navigating.
3096.statement: Forgetting to align north on the compass with north on the map before navigating
3096.correction: Hold the compass next to the arrow representing magnetic north on the map and rotate your body until the arrow on the map and the arrow on the compass line up with north, then keep the map facing that way even when you change direction.

8902.belief: Requirement to keep checking location to ensure on track. Regular stopping and time wasting as a result of re-orientating the map.
8902.statement: Requirement to keep checking location to ensure on track. Regular stopping and time wasting as a result of re-orientating the map.
8902.correction: Thumbing the map means tracing your route as you move along the map to represent where you are on the map at any given time.

10318.belief: When throwing at a target, pupils will often think only of hitting the target and not the consequences of missing it - which often leads to losing more runs through overthrowing it.
10318.statement: When throwing at a target, pupils will often think only of hitting the target and not the consequences of missing it - which often leads to losing more runs through overthrowing it.
10318.correction: Pupils understand the need to back up their teammate as they throw, and the need for the thrower to check that someone is backing up before throwing.

4434.belief: Many pupils do not move their feet in response to the pitch of a ball, instead keeping their feet in the same place throughout. This leads to awkward and ineffective swings at the ball.
4434.statement: Many pupils do not move their feet in response to the pitch of a ball, instead keeping their feet in the same place throughout. This leads to awkward and ineffective swings at the ball.
4434.correction: Using tees slows down the thought process so that footwork can be learned before facing a moving ball. Almost every shot requires some foot movement and the stance should allow for this by being on balls of feet and with knees slightly bent.

1783.belief: The most common error made when beginning to learn how to bowl in cricket is that pupils throw the ball with the elbow bending in the action which is not allowed.
1783.statement: The most common error made when beginning to learn how to bowl in cricket is that pupils throw the ball with the elbow bending in the action which is not allowed.
1783.correction: Pupils need to understand that the action requires a straight arm and this should be emphasised throughout the lesson. It is perhaps a unique throwing action which takes time to adjust to.

6049.belief: Bowling should always be at the same length to be consistent. The phrase 'good length' might be part of the confusion.
6049.statement: Pupils may believe that bowling should always be at the same length to be consistent. The phrase 'good length' might be part of the confusion.
6049.correction: Pupils should understand that as long as it is a legal ball, the length can vary. This is a good way to outwit the batter as different lengths create different challenges and keeps them guessing.

562.belief: As a batting pair, pupils are often poor at communicating when to run, sometimes even oblivious of the need to communicate at all.
562.statement: As a batting pair, pupils are often poor at communicating when to run, sometimes even oblivious of the need to communicate at all.
562.correction: Teach pupils a simple code that they can use and when to use it, to encourage more understanding of the need to communicate.

6044.belief: When they are not batting, they don't need to pay attention to what is happening on the field.
6044.statement: Pupils may believe that when they are not batting, they don't need to pay attention to what is happening on the field.
6044.correction: Being a good team member requires us to encourage our teammates and be aware of what is happening in the game, even when our turn to bat has not finished or even started yet.

10432.belief: A trial is where people are judged to see who makes the cut and who doesn't.
10432.statement: A trial is where people are judged to see who makes the cut and who doesn't.
10432.correction: A trial is an opportunity for everyone to show what they can do and also learn where they could focus on as priority areas for improvement.

2832.belief: Everyone's sprinting technique should look the same.
2832.statement: Everyone's sprinting technique should look the same.
2832.correction: Everyone will have their own natural style of running. Forcing pupils to be too upright for example may be sub optimal for some. Pupils should find their natural position which may include a slight lean.

3289.belief: To get faster at running middle distance you always have to train at race pace.
3289.statement: To get faster at running middle distance you always have to train at race pace.
